newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Nordic currency gains to stay in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nordic currency gains to stay in spotlight.

text.p: Nordic currencies, particularly the Norwegian crown, are expected to continue feeling upward pressure after lively central bank action on Friday ranging from market intervention to high-speed key rate cuts, dealers said.

Norway's central bank, facing a runaway crown, cut official interest rates for the second time in two days on Friday only to see the currency power more than two percent in three days to a new four-year peak of 4.03 per mark at one stage.
Buckling under market pressure, the bank simultaneously announced it would now curb its massive but fruitless interventions and let the crown run its course for a while.
Dealers in Finland, Denmark and Sweden said their central banks had also sold their respective currencies, all of which have also been strengthening recently, for German marks.
The Norwegian and Swedish crowns have each risen more than two percent since January 7. The Danish crown and Finnish markka rises have been notable though less dramatic.

Dollar strength, coupled with strong economic growth prospects, have boosted currencies across the Nordic area although only Norway has so far seen the market test levels significant enough to force key rate cuts.
Oystein Stephansen at S-E Banken in Oslo told Reuters Financial Television the Norwegian central bank's decision to curb interventions would lead to more volatility.

"Markets are going to have a closer look at the crown, possibly test it towards the D-mark. It is a tough call today when the markets are moving very rapidly. We are going to see a new level for the crown," he said.

Sweden's Riksbank, eager to show the currency is stable without being linked to the European Union's Exchange Rate Mechansim (ERM), has already said it would enter the market to iron out sudden crown movements.
"It is a small stake to stop the strengthening of the crown in the international turbulence," one dealer said. "The Riksbank is not worried about the crown in itself."
Dealers said the dollar's recent surge has sparked interest in peripheral currencies, particularly in the Nordic ones because their economies have stronger than average European growth prospects.
Swedish economic think-tank KI forecasts gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 2.7 percent in 1997. Official forecasts for Finland are for GDP growth of up to four percent in 1997.

The Norwegian government said in its budget it expected 1997 GDP growth of 3.1 percent for the overall economy and 2.5 percent excluding oil production. For Denmark, consensus market forecasts are for 1997 GDP of 2.7 percent.
Analysts said these strong fundamentals suggest further gains for the Finnish markka, which has been linked to Europe's ERM since last October.
"On balance, there are strengthening pressures on the markka," SE-Banken's Helsinki chief economist Esko Torsti said.
